Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the Stratos Aerospace Technologies Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. As a reminder, instructions for queuing questions will be provided at that time. Please note this event is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Sarah Thompson, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Thompson:
Thank you, Operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to Stratos Aerospace Technologies' Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. Joining me today are Dr. Elena Vasquez, Chief Executive Officer; John Hargrove, Chief Financial Officer; Michael Chen, Chief Operating Officer; Dr. Lisa Patel, Chief Technology Officer; Robert Kline, Chief Strategy Officer; Jennifer Ruiz, Chief Marketing Officer; and David Moreno, Chief Compliance Officer.

Before we begin, I'd like to remind you that this call contains forward-looking statements. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of risks and uncertainties.

Dr. Elena Vasquez:
Thank you, Sarah, and good morning. Stratos Aerospace Technologies delivered a solid performance in Q3 2024, demonstrating the resilience of our business model and the strength of our diversified portfolio across commercial aerospace, defense, and services. Our priorities remain focused on executing our strategy, driving operational excellence, and delivering value to our shareholders. We've seen strong execution in our priority defense programs, robust gross and operating margins alongside solid net income growth, disciplined capital deployment through dividends, buybacks, and selective acquisitions, balanced revenue growth by segment, favorable geopolitical tailwinds boosting defense spending, meaningful expansion in our service offerings and customer diversification, improved program margins with better cost performance, and an impressive book-to-bill ratio signaling continued backlog growth.

We are particularly excited about the recent advancements in our Next-Generation Air Dominance or NGAD program and its potential to solidify our leadership in air superiority and joint all-domain operations for future growth. We are seeing strong demand for our defense systems, and our commercial aerospace business is recovering steadily as production ramps resume.

John Hargrove:
Thank you, Elena, and good morning, everyone. Now, let's turn to the financials. In Q3 2024, we reported revenue of $12.4 billion, representing an 8% increase year-over-year. Our earnings per share were $2.85. We continue to maintain a strong balance sheet with $5.2 billion in cash and equivalents. Our guidance for the full year remains unchanged at the high end for EPS of $11.20 to $11.50. We are actively managing our costs and investing in key growth initiatives like hypersonics and digital sustainment. We are also focused on returning capital to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases.

Our specific financial highlights include gross margin of 18.7%, operating income reflecting a 12.3% margin, and free cash flow of $2.8 billion projected for the full year.

To provide more depth, let me start with the performance of our priority defense programs, which continue to be the bedrock of Stratos Aerospace Technologies' growth trajectory. In Q3 FY24, these programs delivered $2.8 billion in revenue, up 18% year-over-year and representing 62% of our total segment bookings. Adjusted program EBITA margins expanded to 14.2%, a 110-basis-point improvement from last year, driven by higher-volume low-rate initial production ramps, favorable fixed-price contract settlements, and proactive supply chain mitigation against inflation in titanium and rare earths.

Drilling into key programs, our NGAD platform, where we're in the engineering and manufacturing development phase as a principal subcontractor, saw deliveries of Block 3 test articles hit 125% of plan, with first flight of our integrated sensor fusion suite—incorporating gallium nitride-based active electronically scanned array radars—achieving initial operational capability last month ahead of schedule. This positions us for a $1.2 billion FY25 award under the Joint All-Domain Command and Control indefinite delivery indefinite quantity vehicle. Backlog here stands at $4.7 billion, with foreign military sales opportunities emerging from Indo-Pacific allies amid escalating tensions in the Taiwan Strait. Margins are holding at 13.5%, buffered by our digital twin initiatives that reduced scrap rates by 22% through machine learning-optimized computer numerical control machining.

In hypersonics, our Glide Phase Interceptor program for the Missile Defense Agency saw a major milestone with successful end-to-end flight test number four from Kauai, validating our boost-glide vehicle with Mach 7-plus sustainment and two-to-three kilometer per second terminal divert kinetics. Revenue jumped 32% quarter-over-quarter to $450 million, fueled by a $900 million sole-source contract modification for 48 additional units. We're now scaling production at our Camden, Arkansas facility, where we've implemented a fully automated composites layup line—cutting cycle times 40%—to meet the FY26 preliminary design review. Regional tailwinds are strong: NATO's $10 billion hypersonic gap-filler request for information and Israel's Iron Dome interoperability tests have unlocked $300 million in early foreign military sales commitments. Program margins ticked up to 15.8% on learning curve efficiencies, though we're monitoring engineering, procurement, and construction costs tied to domestic hydroxyl-terminated polybutadiene propellant sourcing.

On the rotary-wing side, our VH-92A Presidential Helicopter sustainment contract with the Marine One program generated $320 million in Q3 revenue, flat year-over-year but with 200 basis points margin expansion to 12.1% via our performance-based logistics framework. We've delivered 95% fleet availability rates, exceeding service level agreements by five points, thanks to our Phoenix predictive maintenance algorithm that leverages edge AI on the T700-GE-701D engines. This program's $2.1 billion backlog includes a new $500 million task order for cyber-hardened mission systems, aligning with U.S. Cyber Command directives.

Unmanned systems remain a high-growth vector. Our MQ-Next loyal wingman drone family—building on the RQ-180 heritage—secured a $1.1 billion Air Force collaborative combat aircraft contract award in September, with initial Block 1 deliveries commencing from our Mojave test bed. Q3 revenue was $280 million, up 45% year-over-year, with gross margins at 16.4% reflecting swarm autonomy software intellectual property monetization. We've integrated our Viper strike package, achieving 98% hit probability in live-fire demos against moving maritime targets. Strategically, this program's penetration into AUKUS Pillar 2 is accelerating, with Australia committing $400 million for 24 airframes, countering People's Republic of China gray-zone activities in the South China Sea.

Finally, space domain awareness under our Proliferated Warfighter Space Architecture contribution hit $510 million in revenue, a 25% year-over-year increase, with six space development and situational responsiveness-3 satellites launched on United Launch Alliance Vulcan Cert-2. Our optical inter-satellite links demonstrated 10 gigabits per second throughput in low Earth orbit, enabling resilient mesh networking for the National Reconnaissance Office's hybrid architecture. Backlog exceeds $3.2 billion, bolstered by Space Development Agency Tranche 2 awards and a $700 million UK Skynet replacement option. Margins here are robust at 17.2%, supported by our Tucson cleanroom expansion and cooperative research and development agreements with Air Force Research Laboratory on quantum-secured communications.

Overall, priority programs ended the quarter with a $28.5 billion backlog—up 14% year-over-year—and a book-to-bill of 1.3 times. Risks remain around Department of Defense topline uncertainty post-continuing resolution, but our 85% domestic content strategy and $500 million in multi-year sustainment wins de-risk the profile. Looking to FY25, we guide $11.5 to $12.2 billion in priority program revenue, with margins expanding to 14.5 to 15.0%, assuming continued NGAD concurrency and hypersonic scale-up.

Geopolitical flashpoints from Ukraine to the Middle East are driving allied spend toward 3.2% of GDP NATO targets, while our intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance-to-strike kill chains align perfectly with Joint Warfighting Concept priorities.

Building on that strong foundation, let's examine our gross margin, operating margin, and net income analysis, which reflect the strength of our execution amid a dynamic aerospace and defense landscape. Gross margin came in at 18.7% for the quarter—expanding 120 basis points year-over-year from 17.5%, and up 40 basis points sequentially from Q2. This marks our strongest quarterly gross margin in over two years and puts us on track for full-year guidance of 18.0% to 18.5%.

The expansion was fueled by improved program execution on fixed-price development contracts, particularly in hypersonics. Our AR-1 hypersonic glide vehicle program saw risk retirements that reduced cost overruns by 15% quarter-over-quarter. We recognized $450 million in favorable contract adjustments here, boosting segment gross margins to 22%.

Supply chain normalization played a big role, with post-COVID titanium and rare-earth sourcing disruptions easing via our just-in-time inventory model—leveraging dual-sourcing from U.S. and allied suppliers like Australia's Lynas Rare Earths—delivering 8% cost of goods sold savings. In commercial aviation, the Boeing 737 MAX ramp-up supported by our nacelle and thrust reverser systems contributed a 250 basis points mix shift, as higher-margin aftermarket services grew 25% to $1.2 billion.

U.S. DoD fixed-price wins under the FY2023 National Defense Authorization Act, including our next-gen unmanned combat aerial vehicle, held steady at 19.5% margins despite inflation. Internationally, Middle East sales—F-15EX wing assemblies for Saudi Arabia—drove 20.2% margins, up from 18% last year, thanks to favorable foreign exchange hedging. Europe lagged at 16.8% due to A400M program delays at Airbus, but we're mitigating with digital twin engineering to accelerate certification.

Offsetting pressure was labor escalation in missile programs, countered with automation like robotic composite layup cells at Huntsville, targeting 200 basis points of future gross margin accretion.

Operating margin expanded to 12.3%—up 90 basis points year-over-year from 11.4% and 30 basis points sequentially. This reflects disciplined operating expense management, with total expenses at 6.4% of revenue, flat year-over-year despite $150 million in incremental research and development.

Key drivers included a 10% reduction in selling, general, and administrative through zero-based budgeting, saving $80 million, and favorable pension adjustments from higher discount rates. Defense systems operating margins hit 14.8%, propelled by our integrated air and missile defense suite, including PAC-3 MSE interceptors, where volume from a $2.5 billion DoD award scaled fixed costs. Space margins improved to 11.2% on GPS III follow-on satellites and Vulcan Centaur contributions. Commercial aviation rebounded to 10.5%, as OEM recovery outpaced costs on 787 fuselage sections.

Asia-Pacific growth—Japan's F-X program—added 50 basis points, while Ukraine urgency boosted European loitering munitions at 15% margins. We absorbed $120 million in one-time intangible amortization from acquisitions, but that's largely behind us.

Net income attributable to shareholders was $1.05 billion, or $2.85 diluted EPS—up 22% from $860 million, or $2.32. Excluding a $200 million discrete tax benefit from research and development credits under the CHIPS Act, adjusted net income was $950 million, or 10.2% net margin. This beat stemmed from margin expansion and interest expense discipline on our $15 billion net debt at 3.8%. Effective tax rate at 21.5%. Free cash flow supported $400 million in repurchases.

Our $125 billion backlog—65% defense, 40% deliverable in 24 months—provides visibility. AI-driven predictive maintenance on C-130J and additive manufacturing for F-35 position us for 100-150 basis points annual margin expansion through FY2025. Risks around other transaction authority delays and tariffs are mitigated by diversification and cost programs.

Next, on revenue by segment—commercial aerospace, defense, and services—our three core segments drove total company revenue of $12.4 billion, up 8% year-over-year. Commercial aerospace delivered strong growth, while defense and services provided balance.

Commercial aerospace came in at $8.2 billion, up 18% year-over-year, or 20% adjusted, driven by OEM deliveries and widebody rebound. Narrowbody like A320neo ramped to 52 units monthly, with 737 MAX shipments up 28%. Widebodies up 25% on 787. North America 55%, Europe 22%, Asia-Pacific 35%. Backlog $320 billion, book-to-bill 1.3x.

Defense at $7.1 billion, up 6% or 8% organic. F-35 lots $2.1 billion up 12%, missiles 15%, unmanned $900 million up 20%, space $1.2 billion up 4%. U.S. DoD 70%, international up 14%. Backlog $210 billion, 1.1x book-to-bill.

Services $3.4 billion, up 14%, beating guide. Commercial MRO 16%, defense 11%. MENA +22%, APAC 18%. Backlog $45 billion, 85% recurring.

This balance de-risks outlook; full-year revenue $72-75 billion affirmed.

Shifting to capital deployment strategy, with adjusted EPS up 12% to $2.85 and $128 billion backlog, our approach is disciplined and shareholder-friendly. We deploy 75-85% of $2.8-3.0 billion free cash flow across dividends, buybacks, and M&A, with net debt-to-EBITDA at 1.2x and $5.2 billion cash.

Dividends: 10% hike to $0.68 quarterly, $2.72 annualized, 2.4% yield—28th year of increases. Payout 45%, targeting 8-10% growth.

Buybacks: $1.1 billion year-to-date on 4.2 million shares, 150 bps EPS accretion. $1.4 billion remaining, $800 million in Q4.

M&A: Three tuck-ins $650 million—cyber, UAV swarm, directed energy—accretive at 8x EBITDA. $5-7 billion dry powder for 2025 deals like European radar for AUKUS.

40% returns to shareholders, 35% M&A, 25% balance sheet. Guidance reaffirmed.

On geopolitical factors affecting defense spending, global spend hit $2.44 trillion in 2023 per SIPRI, up 6.8%, CAGR 4-5% to 2028. Europe: NATO 23/32 at 2%, Germany €100B fund, Poland 4.1% GDP—our air defense up 35%. Ukraine $200B aid boosts munitions. Indo-Pacific: China tensions, AUKUS $368B, Japan Tomahawks—LRASM $2.5B. Middle East: $14B Israel aid, regional $108B up 12%. U.S. $849.8B request. Backlog up 22%, book-to-bill 1.4x. Raised guidance revenues $28.5-29.0B, EPS $14.80-15.20.

Regarding expansion of service offerings and customer base, services revenue grew 28% to $2.8 billion, 42% of backlog. Advanced Digital Sustainment Platform reduced F-35 maintenance 22%, $750M IDIQ. Hypersonic testbed $450M OTA, cyber upgrades $1.2B. Top 10 customers 48% revenue, 180+ total. 14 FMS $6.2B, Saudi $1.8B. North America 55%, Europe €900M UK, Indo-Pacific 45% India $1.1B, Middle East 18%. Services growth 22-25% FY25, book-to-bill 1.45x.

For program margins and cost performance, blended 12.4% up 90 bps. Aeronautics 13.2%, fighter CPI 1.05, cost $92M/airframe. Missiles 11.8%, CPI 1.08, overruns resolved. Space 10.9%. Portfolio CPI 1.04, $620M cost avoidance. Guide 12.5-13% FY24.

Finally, book-to-bill overall 1.22x, backlog $48.7B up 14%. Defense 1.35x, $25.2B backlog. Commercial 1.12x. Space 1.48x, $12.4B. TTM 1.18x above peers.

Michael Chen:
Thank you, John. Operationally, we have seen significant improvements in our supply chain management, allowing us to increase production rates on key programs like NGAD and hypersonics. We are also investing in automation and digital technologies, including robotic layup lines and AI predictive tools, to improve efficiency and reduce costs by up to 40% in cycle times across facilities in Arkansas and Mojave.

Dr. Lisa Patel:
Thank you, Michael. On the technology front, we're making significant strides in next-generation propulsion systems, including scramjet nozzles reaching TRL 7 and quantum-secured comms via AFRL CRADAs. We anticipate these advancements, like GaN AESA and optical inter-satellite links at 10 Gbps, will give us a competitive edge in hypersonics, unmanned swarms, and proliferated space architectures.

Robert Kline:
Thank you, Lisa. From a strategic perspective, we are actively evaluating potential acquisitions in cyber, UAV, and radar to complement our portfolio and expand into AUKUS and GCAP. We are also developing new business models around digital twins and PBL contracts to capture sustainment opportunities in contested logistics and AI autonomy, targeting 5-7% organic growth.

Jennifer Ruiz:
Thank you, Robert. From a marketing perspective, our new branding campaign emphasizing resilient ISR-to-strike capabilities is resonating with DoD and allied customers, driving a 25% increase in pipeline inquiries. We're leveraging digital channels for FMS outreach, with results showing heightened awareness in Indo-Pacific and NATO markets amid rising tensions.

Operator:
Thank you. We will now begin the question and answer session. Our first question comes from Alex Carter with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Alex Carter:
Good morning. Can you provide more color on the book-to-bill ratio overall and by segment?

Dr. Elena Vasquez:
Certainly, Alex. Our overall book-to-bill of 1.22x drove backlog to $48.7 billion, up 14%. Defense at 1.35x with PrSM and hypersonics wins, commercial stabilizing at 1.12x on LEAP and 777X, space exceptional at 1.48x on Mayhem and New Glenn. This visibility supports 8-10% growth in FY25.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Maria Lopez with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Maria Lopez:
Hi, I'm curious about the capital deployment strategy, particularly M&A pipeline?

John Hargrove:
Maria, our three tuck-ins year-to-date are accretive, and with $5-7 billion dry powder, we're eyeing $1.2 billion radar for AUKUS and counter-drone tech. Structured 70/30 cash-stock, tilting 40% to Asia-Pacific for diversification.

Operator:
Our next question comes from David Kim with Barclays. Please go ahead.

David Kim:
Regarding the technology advancements in hypersonics and NGAD?

Dr. Lisa Patel:
David, our Glide Phase Interceptor flight test #4 validated Mach 7+ kinetics, scaling at Camden with 40% faster cycles. NGAD sensor fusion hit IOC early, with digital twins cutting scrap 22%, positioning for $1.2B FY25.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Emily Chen with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Emily Chen:
Question about geopolitical impacts on defense spending?

Robert Kline:
Emily, $2.44T global spend up 6.8%, NATO 23/32 at 2%, Indo-Pacific AUKUS $368B, Middle East up 12%. Our $128B backlog at 1.4x book-to-bill captures this without pull-forwards.

Dr. Elena Vasquez:
Thank you for your questions. In closing, I'm confident in our ability to navigate the current environment and deliver long-term value to our shareholders. We remain focused on our strategic priorities, operational excellence, and innovation.

Sarah Thompson:
Thank you for joining us today. This concludes our earnings call.

Operator:
This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.
